articles.title: How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share
articles.summary: It’s tough to know whether a deal is actually as good as it claims to be. So, we’re sharing the criteria for how we vet and consider deals.
articles.body: For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands big and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them. Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them. Something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case. In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow, an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon. [Media: The group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care. Vetting deals for coverage consideration is a big, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors. With Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover. For products hit by recent price hikes, the new deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example. To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. (You can use them, too!) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool, which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass. We cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge. However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

articles.title: Who left 'Dancing With the Stars' last night? Top scorer suffers shock exit ahead of finale.
articles.summary: A major contender was eliminated despite earning a perfect 60 out of 60 from the judges.
articles.body:
The Dancing With the Stars semifinals ended in a surprise elimination Tuesday night, with one of the competition's strongest performers missing out on a place in the Season 35 finale.

The six remaining couples each performed two routines, with several earning perfect scores from judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli.

But when the judges' scores were combined with viewer votes, the results brought an unexpected end to one couple's journey.

Here's who was eliminated on Nov. 17 and which celebrities are still competing for the mirror ball trophy.

Who left 'Dancing With the Stars' last night?

Grey's Anatomy star Harry Shum Jr. and his professional partner Jenna Johnson were eliminated during the Dancing With the Stars semifinals, despite earning two perfect scores from the judges.

The pair received 30 out of 30 points for their paso doble to Rihanna's "We Found Love" and another 30 for a quickstep to The Zutons' "Valerie," tying with Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov at the top of the leaderboard with 60 points.

The quickstep was a tribute to Shum's late Glee costar Naya Rivera, who performed the song during the musical comedy's second season. Rivera died in a drowning accident in July 2020 at age 33.

"I feel like Dancing With the Stars is synonymous with Glee , and to be able to dance to Naya's version, it means so much to so many people, including myself," Shum told cohost Julianne Hough before receiving his score. "We miss you, baby girl."

The performance left judge Carrie Ann Inaba "speechless," while Bruno Tonioli praised Shum and Johnson as "two equally powered dancers at the peak of their form" following their paso doble. Derek Hough called it "perfection."

But the perfect scores weren't enough to keep Shum and Johnson in the competition. When the judges' scores were combined with viewer votes, the pair were eliminated just one week before the finale.

Shum later told E! News that he felt "oddly at ease" with the result. "I kind of felt like we accomplished everything we wanted to," he said.

Shum, who worked as a professional dancer before finding fame in Glee and Crazy Rich Asians , is the second experienced dancer to make a surprise exit in as many weeks.

Jenna Dewan, who starred opposite Channing Tatum in Step Up and previously worked as a backup dancer for Janet Jackson, was eliminated the previous week despite finishing near the top of the leaderboard. She had also earned a perfect score the week before her departure.

Meanwhile, Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold advanced to the finale despite finishing at the bottom of the semifinal leaderboard with 48 out of 60 points.

The remaining five couples — Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik, Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov, Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas, Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach, and Wood and Arnold — will compete in the Season 35 finale.

articles.title: Rivian spinoff Also pauses e-bike deliveries over battery and software bugs
articles.summary: Rivian spinoff Also has paused deliveries of its TM-B e-bike due to software bugs causing overnight battery drain and charging errors. A firmware update is underway.
articles.body: Also, the mobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has run into another speed bump. The company was already struggling to get its first e-bikes to customers due to a litany of supply chain headaches and the complexity of building a futuristic bike powered almost entirely by software. Now there is a new wrinkle, the company said in an email sent this week to customers, informing them that their wait just got a little longer. Also said it identified “a few software-based issues, such as charging behavior,” affecting some of the Launch Edition versions of its TM-B bikes. As a result, it was pausing customer deliveries until it could work out a solution. “Our team is hard at work on a firmware update to address these issues so that every TM-B owner can enjoy the full product experience we aspire to, beginning with your very first ride,” the email reads. The issues were already popping up on the Also subreddit, where customers were reporting batteries draining overnight for no apparent reason, in some cases dropping from 70 percent to 40 percent or lower over a couple of days. Others noted that the parasitic drain would trigger a “bike issue detected” or “install battery to ride” error on the bike’s display. Trying to plug the battery in would often fail because the bike wouldn’t recognize the battery installed, they said. [Image: The Also TM-B electric bike at the company’s headquarters in Palo Alto, California. Also has paused customer deliveries until it can fix the problem. The company said it had almost shipped out all of its Launch Edition bikes, after which it planned on transitioning to its Performance Edition. But now that timeline will be delayed beyond what Also previously communicated to its customers who are still waiting on their deliveries, Michele Mehl, senior PR manager at Also, says in an email to The Verge. “The team recognizes this means a delay for customers who have already waited longer than expected, but believes it’s the right decision to ensure every TM-B delivers the full product experience we aspire to,” Mehl added. The company plans on sending another update on the delay on November 24th. It’s been clear from the beginning that Also took on an enormous challenge when it set out to build one of the most high-tech, logistically complex e-bikes ever made. The USB-C chargeable batteries, which are available in either 538Wh or 808Wh packs, are supposed to offer up 100 miles of range. But the 240W power delivery exceeds current regulatory guidelines, forcing Also to work with standards groups to establish new safety and testing protocols. In addition, the bike is powered by a pedal-by-wire system, which means there’s no mechanical connection between the pedaling and the movement of the bike. Instead, the rider pedals a generator motor on the crank, which replenishes the battery; a separate traction motor at the rear wheel is software-driven via a Gates Carbon belt drive. Last month, when I asked Also President Chris Yu whether the company bit off more than it can chew with this bike, he pushed back: > I don’t look at it that way at all. If we were to revisit the design, I would do the exact same thing. The largest untapped opportunity isn’t cyclists who already tolerate the current bike experience. It’s the massive demographic of people intrigued by leaving the car behind who haven’t opted in yet. Their hesitations are consistent: fear of theft, avoiding maintenance every two months, wanting seamless navigation and audio, and needing to carry a child without having to buy three different bikes. > Solving those pain points requires a baseline of technology. Just like in automotive EVs, once you use software to personalize the ride and eliminate friction, people opt in. The majority of people attending our test rides haven’t ridden a bicycle in 10 or 15 years. Our goal wasn’t to go overboard; it was determining the minimum amount of innovation needed to create an experience as frictionless as stepping into a Tesla Model Y or Rivian R2.

articles.title: Sony's updated turntable is an easy entry into the world of vinyl | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Sony's updated turntable for beginners features automatic playback, USB connectivity, and aptX Adaptive Bluetooth.
articles.body:
Record players and other retro tech are making a strong comeback, and I’ve recently rejoined the world of vinyl collecting. Lately, I’ve noticed myself turning to Spotify less frequently, so it felt like the perfect time to start using a record player again.

Choosing a turntable can be quite overwhelming, especially for beginners. That’s where Sony’s new PS-LX3BT turntable comes in.

Since 2019, Sony’s PS-LX310BT has been a go-to choice for vinyl newbies. Now that it has been discontinued, the PS-LX3BT emerges as its successor, keeping the same beginner-friendly approach while adding a few modern upgrades.

Currently priced at $399.99, the PS-LX3BT is designed for people who want to enjoy vinyl without getting too caught up in the technical side of things. It’s also a good option for those looking to upgrade from their first inexpensive turntable without having to learn how to set up or customize a more complicated audio system.

One of its biggest selling points is how easy it is to use. The PS-LX3BT features automatic playback, so you simply press start and the tonearm lifts, moves into position, and drops onto the first track for you. There’s no need to manually position the needle or worry about getting everything just right. It’s a small convenience, but one that makes the experience much less intimidating for newcomers.

Sony has also made a few welcome changes compared with its predecessor. The PS-LX3BT now uses USB-C for power and supports Qualcomm’s aptX Adaptive Bluetooth codec, allowing it to transmit audio at up to 24-bit/96kHz. It also has a traditional phono output alongside Bluetooth, so you can choose between a wired speaker setup and listening wirelessly.

One slightly strange design decision, however, is the repositioning of the start, stop, and tonearm buttons. On the older model, these were placed outside the dust cover. Now they’re underneath it, meaning you’ll have to lift the cover just to press start. It’s not a huge inconvenience, but still kind of annoying.

The turntable also offers USB connectivity for digitizing your vinyl collection. Connect it to a computer, and you can convert your records into digital audio files, which is useful if you want to preserve older records or listen to your collection on the go.

My biggest disappointment is the lack of a built-in speaker. It would have been nice to have everything included for someone just getting started. You’ll need to buy speakers (and possibly an amplifier) or compatible Bluetooth headphones separately, so keep that added cost in mind.

If you’re searching for a more affordable and beginner-friendly automatic record player, there are cheaper options, such as this $179 option from Audio-Technica. But overall, Sony’s PS-LX3BT is a solid choice for anyone ready to dive into the world of vinyl for the first time.

articles.title: Shelly’s new smart valve shuts off your home’s water before a leak becomes a flood
articles.summary: Shelly’s Neo Smart Water Valve turns off the water to your home when a sensor detects a leak while also monitoring water usage and pressure.
articles.body: After releasing a $28 leak sensor earlier this year that conveniently runs off a battery for two years, Shelly is announcing an accompanying smart valve you can install on your home’s main water line to automatically turn off the flow when one of those sensors detects a problem. The Shelly Neo Smart Water Valve is available now through the company’s online store for $499.99, plus the cost of installation if you don’t trust your plumbing skills. It’s not a cheap solution, but it’s cheaper than the fallout of a leak turning into a disaster. The Neo Smart Water Valve is designed to be installed on a standard US 1-inch thread connection (the company plans to launch additional size options next year) and is made from brass so it’s safe to use on plumbing carrying drinking water. It has an IPX7 waterproof rating so the valve will keep working if flooding means it ends up submerged. However, the valve lacks a battery of its own and requires a connection to a power source through an included USB adapter cable. Connecting it to a waterproof power bank instead of an outlet may be the best approach to ensure it still works during a power outage. The smart valve connects to other devices over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth and is designed to integrate into existing smart home setups using webhooks, MQTT, or scripting for advanced users. In addition to shutting off the flow of water into your home in about 12 seconds, the valve also features an ultrasonic measurement system that tracks pressure, flow rate, your home’s consumption, and even the temperature of the water. Through the Shelly app, you can monitor all of that data in order to spot unusual usage patterns that could indicate a wasteful leak, or ensure the pressure doesn’t get high enough to damage pipes or appliances.

articles.title: ABC News quietly suspended staffers behind botched story on Trump sons' business dealings
articles.summary: ABC News quietly sidelined two staffers behind the botched Anduril report involving Donald Trump Jr., while a spokesperson says no one's employment status has changed.
articles.body: ABC News quietly suspended staffers involved in the botched story last month suggesting impropriety in the Trump sons' business dealings, Fox News Digital has confirmed. The Disney-owned network stirred controversy with its report headlined, "Trump sons' investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election," alleging that Anduril, the company investing in a new Baltimore shipyard, had ties to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump through 1789 Capital, a venture capital firm. The report claimed the firm had a "major stake" in Anduril, which was ultimately false. ABC News raised eyebrows when it deleted the report without explanation after the story was called out on social media, then quietly republished a revised version of the report with an editor's note acknowledging the error. GOP SENATOR CALLS FOR FCC PROBE OF ABC NEWS OVER TRUMP SONS-ANDURIL 'POLITICAL HIT JOB' The ordeal resulted in an internal probe to determine what went wrong. While two staffers behind the botched story were reprimanded and rumors they will be terminated swirl, an ABC News spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "No one's employment status has changed." ABC News declined further comment. The Wall Street Journal's Joe Flint first reported that the two staffers were on "paid leave." ABC News' original story wrote, "1789 Capital — a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders — claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company." "Since that investment, Anduril has been awarded 135 other contracts with the U.S. government and to date has received around $1.8 billion from those agreements, according to active defense contracts posted to SAM.gov, the official system for government contracting," the story continued. "The company is one of the largest manufacturers to receive an investment from Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump, but they are not the only one." ABC NEWS QUIETLY REPUBLISHES GUTTED VERSION OF STORY ON TRUMP SONS IT HAD DELETED WITHOUT EXPLANATION Alexa Henning, a spokesperson for 1789 Capital and a former chief of staff to the director of national intelligence, took to social media, insisting the company does not have a "major stake" in Anduril and blasting the "biased hit piece." "Here's a small lesson, that I also explained to ABC, the ‘reporter’ who is a complete idiot conflated raising funds with investment by 1789. Those are two separate actions," Henning reacted at the time. "Meaning the ‘investments’ mentioned were actually the total number raised for a funding round, that MANY companies contribute to," Henning continued. "Another thing that the reporter buried the lead on was that many of these companies have gotten government contracts during Biden AND Trump, which completely negates the assertion by ABC that Don Jr and Eric Trump are doing anything wrong." VENTURE CAPITAL FIRM TIED TO DONALD TRUMP JR WEIGHS LEGAL ACTION AGAINST ABC NEWS OVER BOTCHED REPORT ABC News then sparked confusion among critics when it deleted the entire story, only to republish an overhauled version of the story days later with the new headline reading, "New shipyard announced amid earlier Democratic concerns about potential conflicts of interest" while stressing to readers that Trump Jr. "is not involved in investment decisions." "CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies," the editor's note read at the top of the article. "After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events." Henning has said that nobody from ABC News asked 1789 for comment prior to the initial story being published and that an ABC News journalist "vigorously defended" the report before it was suddenly deleted. She also previously said the company was considering legal action against the Disney-owned news organization. "This should be a cautionary tale for any other reporters who continue to traffic in this false narrative," Henning told Fox News Digital on Wednesday when asked if a lawsuit is still being considered. articles.title: Google is forcing Android app developers to properly support foldables
articles.summary: Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. Games will have to meet requirements starting in August 2027.
articles.body: Now that Apple’s foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables are a good experience. Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. If they don’t, developers risk not being able to publish or update their apps or have reduced visibility for their apps on Google Play. Google says Android apps must meet its “Tier 3 — Adaptive ready” standard. “Apps must fill the available display area without letterboxing or compatibility modes,” Google says. “Apps must preserve state (scroll position, text input, media playback) during rotation, folding/unfolding, and resizing, while supporting multi-window environments.” (The other two tiers are “Adaptive optimized” and “Adaptive differentiated” and take further advantage of the possibilities of foldables.) As of the April 2027 deadline, developers also will have to include three foldable screenshots for their app listings. Developers can start publishing their foldable screenshots today. Similar requirements will apply to games, though developers have until August 2027 to get their titles ready for Android foldables, Google says. (Google “plans to extend” its requirements to other large-screen devices like tablets and Googlebook laptops in “future phases.”) However, game developers will still need to share three foldable screenshots for app listings starting in April. The changes are being announced just weeks after Apple launched the iPhone Duo, which already has more than 200,000 optimized apps, though some developers are still figuring out Apple’s foldable form factor.

articles.title: The first Nvidia RTX Spark mini PCs launch today from Asus, Dell, and MSI
articles.summary: Asus, Dell, and MSI launched the first mini PCs with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip, available starting today.
articles.body: After the first RTX Spark laptops launched earlier this year, Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X chip is also now available in desktops from Asus, Dell, and MSI. More RTX Spark desktops are coming later from Acer, Gigabyte, and HP, while Microsoft’s Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is slated to start shipping this month. The new mini PCs include a 6144-core Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU, 20-core Nvidia Grace CPU, and up to 128GB of memory. That high-end hardware comes with a price to match — Asus’s ProArt GR1X starts at $4,499 for a configuration with 64GB of memory and 1TB of storage. Like the RTX Spark laptops that compete with the MacBook Pro and the DGX Spark desktop Nvidia launched last year, the new mini PCs are Mac Mini or Mac Studio alternatives for developers working with local AI models, as well as RTX-accelerated software. That includes the AI-powered features for tools like Adobe Premiere and Photoshop, and new DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support in Blender 5.3. They can run games too, and Windows on Arm game support is improving, but at these prices, that’s not a realistic reason to pick one up yet. Nvidia says they can act as a “dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents,” and deliver “up to 1 petaflop of AI performance.” They also feature native CUDA support and access to Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux.
